questions.stem: A winery wants to know whether storage temperature affects how quickly the ethanoic acid content of an opened wine rises. Which inquiry question best deconstructs this problem into something testable?
options: How does storage temperature affect the change in ethanoic acid concentration over 7 days?
Is it better for an opened bottle of wine to be stored somewhere cold or somewhere warm?
Which wines turn into vinegar fastest after they have been opened and left on the bench?
Why does an opened bottle of wine taste sour if it is left out for a long period of time?
questions.explanation: A testable inquiry question names one independent variable (storage temperature) and a measurable dependent variable (ethanoic acid concentration over a set time). Asking which storage is 'better' or why wine tastes sour gives no measurable outcome to compare.

questions.stem: Which statement is a hypothesis rather than an inquiry question?
options: Measure the time for a magnesium strip to dissolve in 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid.
Increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid will decrease the time for a magnesium strip to dissolve.
What is the effect of hydrochloric acid concentration on the time for a magnesium strip to dissolve?
Hydrochloric acid reacts with magnesium metal to produce magnesium chloride solution and hydrogen gas.
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable prediction of how the independent variable affects the dependent variable. The question form is an inquiry question, the equation statement is a known fact, and the instruction is part of a method.

questions.stem: A student investigates how the mass of calcium carbonate chips affects the volume of carbon dioxide collected in 2 minutes when the chips are added to 50 mL of hydrochloric acid. What is the dependent variable?
options: The mass of calcium carbonate chips added to the flask
The 50 mL volume of hydrochloric acid used in each trial
The 2 minute period over which the gas is collected
The volume of carbon dioxide collected in 2 minutes
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured in response to the change, here the volume of gas. The mass of chips is the independent variable, and the acid volume and time are factors held constant.

questions.stem: In the same calcium carbonate investigation, why must the size of the chips be held constant?
options: Smaller chips cannot be weighed accurately, so their mass would have to be estimated in each trial
Chip size changes the surface area, which affects the rate and so the volume of gas collected in 2 minutes
Larger chips contain a different compound from smaller chips, which would change the gas produced
Chip size determines the concentration of the acid, so the acid would be different in each trial
questions.explanation: Surface area affects how quickly calcium carbonate reacts, so uncontrolled chip size would change the gas volume independently of the mass. Chips of any size are still calcium carbonate, and chip size has no effect on the acid's concentration.

questions.stem: A student measures how temperature affects the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction using potato extract from potatoes bought on different days. Which factor is the hardest to control, and why?
options: Catalase activity in the extract, since potatoes vary naturally in enzyme content
The temperature of the water bath, since it cannot be read with any thermometer
The volume of hydrogen peroxide, since liquids cannot be measured to better than 1 L
The time of each trial, since a stopwatch cannot be started at a chosen moment
questions.explanation: Biological material varies from sample to sample, so the enzyme content of the extract is a factor that may not be able to be controlled; it should be acknowledged as a limitation. Temperature, volume and time can all be controlled with standard equipment.

questions.stem: Why is it good practice to state the type and amount of data to be collected when designing an investigation?
options: It guarantees that the results will support the hypothesis when the data are analysed
It removes the need to identify any variables to be held constant during the experiment
It allows the results to be reported without units because the data type is already known
It shows in advance how many measurements and repeats will be enough to answer the question
questions.explanation: Planning the data (for example, five concentrations with three trials each) ensures enough evidence is gathered to identify a trend and judge reliability. Planning cannot guarantee that the results support a hypothesis.

questions.stem: A method for finding the enthalpy of solution of ammonium chloride says to 'add some salt to some water and see what happens to the temperature'. Which improvement makes the method most repeatable?
options: Use a larger beaker so that the temperature change is spread through more water during mixing
Ask another student to perform the method instead so that the observer is no longer a factor
Specify the mass of salt, the volume of water, the container and how the temperature is read
Repeat the procedure several times and record whichever temperature change seems most typical
questions.explanation: A repeatable method states the quantities, apparatus and measurement procedure so anyone can reproduce it. Picking the 'most typical' result is selective, and a larger beaker without stated quantities is still vague.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a safety data sheet (SDS) when planning a chemistry investigation?
options: To give the hazards, safe handling, first aid and disposal information for a chemical
To give the concentration of every solution that the class will use in the investigation
To give the expected results of the investigation so that errors can be detected early
To give the price and supplier of a chemical so that the cost of the method can be planned
questions.explanation: An SDS sets out a chemical's hazards, handling and storage, first aid, spill response and disposal. It is not a source of expected results or concentrations for a particular investigation.

questions.stem: A student plans to dispose of leftover copper(II) sulfate solution after an experiment. Which action is consistent with safe and responsible practice?
options: Leave it in an unlabelled beaker on the bench for the next class to use as they need
Pour it onto the school garden because copper is an essential nutrient for plants
Pour it into the labelled heavy-metal waste container as directed by the SDS and teacher
Pour it down the sink with plenty of running water because it is only a dilute solution
questions.explanation: Copper(II) compounds are harmful to aquatic life, so they are collected as heavy-metal waste rather than poured down the drain. Dilution does not remove the environmental hazard, and unlabelled containers are a safety risk.

questions.stem: A student wants to survey classmates about how often they use cleaning products and then report the results. Which ethical consideration applies most directly?
options: Using a fume cupboard when the survey results are collated and analysed
Diluting the cleaning products so the survey can be completed safely
Obtaining informed consent and keeping individual responses confidential
Wearing safety glasses while the survey questions are written and printed
questions.explanation: Collecting data from people requires their informed consent and protection of their privacy. The other options are laboratory safety measures that do not apply to a survey.

questions.stem: A student needs to add exactly 20.00 mL of a standard solution to a conical flask. Which piece of equipment is fit for this purpose?
options: A 20.00 mL volumetric pipette
A 25 mL measuring cylinder
A 50 mL beaker with graduations
A 100 mL conical flask
questions.explanation: A volumetric pipette delivers a fixed volume to two decimal places in millilitres. Measuring cylinders and beakers have much coarser graduations, so they cannot give 20.00 mL.

questions.stem: Balance X reads to 0.1 g and balance Y reads to 0.001 g. Which statement is correct?
options: Both balances have the same resolution, so either suits any mass measurement
Balance Y has the finer resolution, so it detects smaller changes in mass
Balance X has the finer resolution, so it detects smaller changes in mass
Balance Y is more accurate, so its readings must be closer to the true value
questions.explanation: Resolution is the smallest change an instrument can show, so the balance reading to 0.001 g has the finer resolution. A fine resolution does not guarantee accuracy, since a badly calibrated balance can still read wrongly.

questions.stem: Which of these is secondary data?
options: Temperatures a student reads while heating water over a spirit burner in class
Masses of precipitate a student weighs after filtering and drying in a practical
Enthalpy of combustion values for alcohols taken from a published data book
Titres a student records while titrating vinegar samples in a school laboratory
questions.explanation: Secondary data are collected by someone else, such as values in a data book or journal. Measurements the student makes personally are primary data.

questions.stem: Which column heading in a results table follows SI conventions for a volume measured with a burette?
options: Volume of NaOH added in mls
NaOH added (amount)
Volume (ml's) of NaOH added
Volume of NaOH added (mL)
questions.explanation: A column heading names the quantity and gives its unit in brackets with the correct symbol, mL. 'mls' and 'ml's' are incorrect forms, and 'amount' gives no unit at all.

questions.stem: A student measures the mass of magnesium oxide formed from five different masses of magnesium. Which way of presenting the results is most appropriate?
options: A bar chart with one bar for each trial, ordered from smallest to largest mass
A scatter graph joining each point dot to dot, mass of oxide on the horizontal axis
A scatter graph with a line of best fit, mass of magnesium on the horizontal axis
A pie chart showing the share of the total magnesium oxide made in each trial
questions.explanation: Two continuous variables are shown on a scatter graph with a line of best fit, and the independent variable goes on the horizontal axis. Joining points dot to dot implies each wobble is real rather than random error.

questions.stem: How many significant figures are in the measurement 0.03070 mol?
options: Three
Five
Six
Four
questions.explanation: Leading zeros only place the decimal point, so they are not significant. The digits 3, 0, 7 and the trailing 0 after the decimal point are significant, giving four.

questions.stem: Use c = n/V. A student dissolves 0.0215 mol of solute to make 250.0 mL of solution. How should the concentration be reported?
options: 0.0860 mol mL⁻¹
0.0860 mol L⁻¹
0.086 mol L⁻¹
questions.explanation: 0.0215 ÷ 0.2500 = 0.0860 mol L⁻¹. The amount has three significant figures (the fewest in the data), so the answer is given to three; 0.086 has only two, and mol mL⁻¹ is the wrong unit for this value.

questions.stem: Use Q = mcΔT with c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. 150.0 g of water warms by 12.4 °C. What is Q, to an appropriate number of significant figures?
options: 7.8 kJ
questions.explanation: Q = 150.0 × 4.18 × 12.4 = 7774.8 J = 7.77 kJ. The specific heat and temperature change each have three significant figures, so three are kept; 77.7 kJ is a factor of ten too large.

questions.stem: A flow diagram is drawn for an investigation that makes copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide and sulfuric acid. What is the main advantage of this representation?
options: It shows the sequence of steps and the materials entering and leaving each step
It shows the exact masses of every product formed at each step of the process
It replaces the need to write a balanced equation for the reaction taking place
It shows the random and systematic errors that will occur during each step
questions.explanation: Flow diagrams display the order of steps and what goes in and out of each, which makes a procedure easy to follow. They do not give quantities or errors, and the balanced equation is still needed for calculations.

questions.stem: In a reaction, 2.0 g of magnesium combines with 1.3 g of oxygen. Assuming the same mass ratio, what mass of oxygen combines with 6.0 g of magnesium?
questions.explanation: The ratio is 1.3/2.0 = 0.65 g of oxygen per gram of magnesium, so 6.0 × 0.65 = 3.9 g. Multiplying 1.3 by 6.0, or dividing 6.0 by 0.65, ignores the ratio.

questions.stem: The solubility of a salt was measured at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C and lies on a smooth curve. Finding the solubility at 45 °C from the curve is an example of:
options: calibration of the thermometer used in the experiment
interpolation within the range of the measured data
extrapolation beyond the range of the measured data
a systematic error introduced by reading the graph
questions.explanation: Reading a value between measured points is interpolation, which is generally reliable. Extrapolation means extending the trend beyond the measured range, where it may not hold.

questions.stem: A student's data show the rate of a reaction rising steadily from 10 °C to 40 °C. The student predicts the rate at 90 °C by extending the line. Why should this prediction be treated with caution?
options: Extending a straight line always gives an answer that is too high, by a predictable amount
A graph cannot be used to find a value unless it lies exactly on one of the plotted points
The trend may not continue outside the measured range, for example if a reactant evaporates
Rates of reaction always decrease above 50 °C, so the line must curve downward after that
questions.explanation: Extrapolation assumes the relationship continues unchanged beyond the data, which may not happen (a reactant may boil off or decompose, or an enzyme may denature). Rates do not always fall above 50 °C, and interpolating between points is valid.

questions.stem: Titres of 19.85, 19.90, 20.45 and 19.80 mL are recorded. Which value should be reported as the mean titre?
questions.explanation: The 20.45 mL titre is not concordant, so it is excluded. The mean of 19.85, 19.90 and 19.80 mL is 19.85 mL; including the outlier gives 20.00 mL.

questions.stem: Marble chips react with hydrochloric acid, and the mass of the flask falls by 0.88 g in the first 40 s. What is the mean rate of mass loss over this period?
options: 35 g s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Mean rate = change in mass ÷ time = 0.88 ÷ 40 = 0.022 g s⁻¹. Dividing time by mass, or ignoring time altogether, gives the other values.

questions.stem: Graph data show that as the concentration of a reactant doubles from 0.10 to 0.20 mol L⁻¹, the initial rate doubles, and from 0.20 to 0.40 mol L⁻¹ it doubles again. Which relationship do the data suggest?
options: The initial rate is independent of the concentration of the reactant used
The initial rate is directly proportional to the concentration of the reactant
The initial rate is inversely proportional to the concentration of the reactant
The initial rate increases with the square of the concentration of the reactant
questions.explanation: When doubling one variable doubles the other each time, the two are directly proportional. A square relationship would make the rate four times larger for each doubling.

questions.stem: A pH meter is calibrated with a buffer that has been contaminated and every reading is 0.3 units too high. What type of error is this?
options: An uncontrolled factor, because pH meters cannot be calibrated
No error, because the readings are all consistent with each other
A systematic error, shifting every reading in the same direction
A random error, scattering readings above and below the true value
questions.explanation: A fault that shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction is a systematic error. Random errors scatter readings unpredictably, and consistent readings can still all be wrong.

questions.stem: Which action reduces the effect of random error on a titration result?
options: Choosing an indicator that changes colour well after the equivalence point
Performing more titrations and averaging the concordant titres
Using the same faulty burette for every titration in the set
Recording each titre to fewer decimal places than the burette shows
questions.explanation: Random errors vary in size and direction, so averaging several concordant results reduces their effect. Repeating with the same faulty equipment does nothing to a systematic error and nothing extra for random error.

questions.stem: Two groups measure the enthalpy of combustion of ethanol. Group A uses a copper can and group B an aluminium can; both get closely agreeing values that are well below the data book value. What does repeating the experiment with different equipment help to show?
options: Whether the data book value for ethanol has been printed incorrectly
Whether the ethanol in each spirit burner is the same compound or not
Whether a systematic error, such as heat loss, is built into the method
Whether the random error in each group's readings has been eliminated
questions.explanation: If different equipment gives the same low value, the error is likely built into the method, such as heat lost to the surroundings, which is systematic. Agreement within a group reflects precision and says nothing about systematic error.

questions.stem: A student carries out a rate experiment over a whole afternoon in a laboratory whose air temperature rises from 19 °C to 27 °C. How is the changing air temperature best described?
options: The independent variable that the student has deliberately chosen to test
The dependent variable that the student measures in each trial
A systematic error caused by poor resolution of the stopwatch
An uncontrolled factor that is a source of uncertainty in the results
questions.explanation: A factor that changes during an investigation without being deliberately varied is an uncontrolled factor, and it adds uncertainty. It is not the variable being tested or the one measured.

questions.stem: A student's four titres are 24.10, 24.15, 24.10 and 24.05 mL, but the true titre is 22.40 mL. How are the results best described?
options: Accurate but not precise
Both accurate and precise
Neither accurate nor precise
Precise but not accurate
questions.explanation: The titres agree closely with each other, so they are precise. They are all about 1.7 mL above the true value, so they are not accurate, which points to a systematic error.

questions.stem: A student tests whether salt concentration affects the boiling point of water using only one sample at each concentration. Why are the conclusions limited?
options: Salt concentration should have been the dependent variable in this design
A sample size of one gives no way to judge whether results are reliable
Boiling points cannot be measured with any thermometer in a school laboratory
Using one sample at each concentration makes all the results more accurate
questions.explanation: With one trial per concentration, a random error cannot be recognised, so reliability cannot be judged. Repeating trials or using more samples would show whether results are consistent.

questions.stem: A student claims to have measured how temperature affects reaction rate, but also used a more concentrated acid for the higher-temperature trials. What is the main problem?
options: The results are not valid, because two variables changed at once
The results are not precise, because the readings must be scattered
The results are not reliable, because the trials were not repeated
The results contain a systematic error caused by the thermometer
questions.explanation: Validity requires that only the independent variable is changed, so the effect on the dependent variable can be attributed to it. Changing concentration as well means the effect of temperature cannot be separated out.

questions.stem: In a trial of three catalysts, catalyst X gave the fastest rate in two of three repeats and catalyst Y in the third. Which conclusion is best justified?
options: No conclusion of any kind can be made, so the investigation should simply be abandoned
Catalyst X may be the most effective, but more trials are needed before a firm conclusion
Catalyst X is definitely the most effective catalyst for this reaction under all conditions
Catalyst Y is the most effective because its single fastest result was the largest value
questions.explanation: The evidence leans towards catalyst X but is not definitive, so a conclusion should be stated tentatively with its limitations and a suggestion for further trials. Overstating a conclusion or ignoring the data are both unjustified.

questions.stem: How does a reference list differ from a bibliography?
options: A reference list gives only sources cited in the text; a bibliography may include other sources consulted
A reference list gives sources consulted but not cited; a bibliography gives only sources cited in the text
A reference list is used only for websites; a bibliography is used only for books and printed journals
A reference list is placed at the start of a report; a bibliography is placed at the end of a report
questions.explanation: A reference list contains the sources actually cited in the work, while a bibliography can also list background sources that were read but not cited. Both can contain any type of source.

questions.stem: IUPAC sets international rules for naming compounds and for symbols and units. Which key idea of science as a human endeavour does this illustrate?
options: Scientific models are always replaced as soon as new technologies appear
The acceptance of science depends mainly on its economic value
Scientific knowledge cannot be applied outside the laboratory
Science relies on international conventions for clear communication
questions.explanation: Agreed naming and symbol conventions let chemists everywhere communicate without ambiguity, which is part of communication and collaboration. The other statements misstate how science develops and is used.

questions.stem: The model of the atom changed as evidence from discharge tubes, alpha-particle scattering and emission spectra emerged. Which key idea does this illustrate?
options: Scientific models are fixed once they have been published in a journal
New evidence is accepted only if it agrees with the existing model
Models are reviewed and modified as new evidence and technologies emerge
A model is abandoned whenever a single scientist disagrees with it
questions.explanation: Each new line of evidence, often made possible by new technology, led to refinements of the atomic model; this is the development concept. Models are not fixed, nor discarded on the word of one person.

questions.stem: CFCs were adopted as safe, unreactive refrigerants, but were later found to damage the stratospheric ozone layer and were phased out internationally. Which key idea does this best illustrate?
options: A chemical found to be unreactive in the laboratory can never cause harm
International collaboration cannot help to solve environmental problems
Applications of science can have unexpected consequences that need monitoring
Scientific knowledge is unaffected by social and political considerations
questions.explanation: CFCs illustrate application and limitation: a beneficial use had unforeseen harmful effects that were found through monitoring and then addressed. The international phase-out also contradicts the claim that collaboration cannot help.

questions.stem: A government delays approving a new pesticide while community groups debate its safety, even though trials show low toxicity. Which key idea does this illustrate?
options: Community debate always shows that the scientific evidence was flawed
Acceptance of science can be influenced by social and ethical considerations
Scientific trials are only valid once the public has voted to accept them
Toxicity data are secondary data and therefore cannot be used in decisions
questions.explanation: The influence concept recognises that social, economic, cultural and ethical factors affect whether scientific knowledge is accepted and used. Public debate does not change the validity of trial data, nor does it prove the data wrong.
